## Description

This vignette shows how to generate data points from a niche using functions in the `nicheR` package. The data points represent the sites or conditions where a virtual species was observed, and the way to generate them depends on the data available:

- `virtual_data()`: draws points directly from the ellipsoid. No environmental data are needed (virtual mode).
- `sample_data()`: draws points from a prediction of the niche, which can be a raster or a table (spatial and tabular modes).
- `sample_biased_data()`: draws points from a prediction that was combined with sampling bias (spatial mode).

For the ideas behind this step, see [Generating data](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/concepts.html#generating-data) in the Concepts vignette.

<br>

## Getting ready

If `nicheR` has not been installed yet, please do so. See the [Main guide](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/index.html) for installation instructions.

Use the following lines of code to load `nicheR` and other packages needed for this vignette, and to set a working directory (if necessary).

<u>Note</u>: We will display functions from other packages as `package::function()`.

```{r get_ready, results='hide', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Load packages
library(nicheR)
library(terra)

# Current directory
getwd()

# Define new directory
#setwd("YOUR/DIRECTORY")  # modify if setting a new directory

# Saving original plotting parameters
original_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
```

<br>

## Loading example data

The lines of code below load the data used in this vignette. The data are included in the `nicheR` package and were obtained in the previous vignettes:

- The reference niche, defined by two environmental variables (bio1: Mean Annual Temperature and bio12: Annual Precipitation). It was built with `cl = 0.99` instead of the default 0.95, so its boundary reaches the ranges it was built from (see [The niche as an ellipsoid](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/concepts.html#the-niche-as-an-ellipsoid)). See [1. Build ellipsoid](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/creating_ellipsoid_based_niches.html).
- The environmental conditions in part of the Americas, as a table, to represent the background.
- A prediction of the reference niche for the same region. See [2. Make a prediction](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/predict.html).
- The same prediction combined with sampling bias. See [3. Working with bias](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/bias.html).

```{r data}
# Reference niche
data("ref_ellipse", package = "nicheR")

# Background data
data("back_data", package = "nicheR")

# Prediction of the reference niche
pred_rast <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "predictions_rast.tif",
                                     package = "nicheR"))

# Prediction combined with sampling bias
biased_rast <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "applied_bias_rast.tif",
                                       package = "nicheR"))
```

<br>

Let's check the layers in the two rasters. We will use their names to tell the functions which layer to sample from.

```{r data_check}
# Layers in the prediction
names(pred_rast)

# Layer in the biased prediction
names(biased_rast)
```

<br>

## Generating virtual data

The `virtual_data()` function generates points using only the ellipsoid. The points are drawn from the multivariate normal distribution defined by the centroid and the covariance matrix of the niche. Below we show a general example of how to use this function.

```{r virtual}
# Generating virtual data
virt_data <- virtual_data(object = ref_ellipse, n = 1000)

# Check the first points
head(virt_data)
```

<br>

The result has one row per point and one column per variable of the niche. The points have environmental values only. They have no coordinates, because no geography is involved.

Now let's plot the points with the reference niche. We will use `plot_ellipsoid()` to plot the ellipsoid and `add_data()` to add the points.

```{r virtual_plot}
# Variables and axis limits for the plots
vars <- c("bio_1", "bio_12")
xlim_v <- c(18.5, 28.5)
ylim_v <- c(700, 2800)

# Plotting the virtual data
mars <- c(4, 4, 2, 1)
par(mar = mars)  # adjust margins for better visualization

plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, lwd = 2,
               xlim = xlim_v, ylim = ylim_v,
               xlab = "Bio1 (Mean Annual Temperature)",
               ylab = "Bio12 (Annual Precipitation)",
               main = "Virtual Data from the Reference Niche")

add_data(virt_data, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#0004d5", pch = 16, cex = 0.5)
```

<br>

As you can see, there are more points near the centroid, and they become fewer toward the boundary of the ellipsoid.

<br>

### Effect of the truncate argument

In the plot above, a few points are outside the ellipsoid. The normal distribution has no limits, and the boundary of this niche encloses `r round(ref_ellipse$cl * 100, 1)`% of it, so about `r round((1 - ref_ellipse$cl) * 100, 1)`% of the points are expected outside. The argument `truncate` controls whether those points are kept.

```{r truncate}
# Points are generated only inside the ellipsoid
virt_trunc <- virtual_data(object = ref_ellipse, n = 1000, truncate = TRUE)
```

<br>

Let's plot the two sets of points to visualize the effect of the argument `truncate`.

```{r truncate_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting the virtual data
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), cex = 0.6, mar = mars)  # set up the plotting area

## Not truncated
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, lwd = 2,
               xlim = xlim_v, ylim = ylim_v,
               xlab = "Bio1 (Mean Annual Temperature)",
               ylab = "Bio12 (Annual Precipitation)",
               main = "truncate = FALSE")

add_data(virt_data, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#0004d5", pch = 16, cex = 0.5)

## Truncated
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, lwd = 2,
               xlim = xlim_v, ylim = ylim_v,
               xlab = "Bio1 (Mean Annual Temperature)",
               ylab = "Bio12 (Annual Precipitation)",
               main = "truncate = TRUE")

add_data(virt_trunc, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#0004d5", pch = 16, cex = 0.5)
```

<br>

With `truncate = TRUE`, all the points are inside the ellipsoid. Use this option when the boundary is meant to be a hard limit for the species.

<br>

### Effect of the sampling argument in virtual data

The argument `sampling` controls how the points are distributed inside the ellipsoid. There are three options:

- `"centroid"`: more points near the centroid. This is the default.
- `"edge"`: more points near the boundary.
- `"uniform"`: points spread evenly through the ellipsoid.

The options `"edge"` and `"uniform"` need a boundary to work with, so they can only be used with `truncate = TRUE`.

```{r virtual_sampling}
# More points near the centroid
virt_cent <- virtual_data(object = ref_ellipse, n = 500, truncate = TRUE,
                          sampling = "centroid")

# More points near the boundary
virt_edge <- virtual_data(object = ref_ellipse, n = 500, truncate = TRUE,
                          sampling = "edge")

# Points spread evenly
virt_unif <- virtual_data(object = ref_ellipse, n = 500, truncate = TRUE,
                          sampling = "uniform")
```

<br>

Let's check the three sets of points with a plot.

```{r virtual_sampling_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.5, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting the virtual data
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), cex = 0.75, mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2, 0.5))

## Centroid
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, lwd = 2, xlim = xlim_v, ylim = ylim_v,
               xlab = "Bio1", ylab = "Bio12", main = "centroid")

add_data(virt_cent, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#0004d5", pch = 16, cex = 0.4)

## Edge
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, lwd = 2, xlim = xlim_v, ylim = ylim_v,
               xlab = "Bio1", ylab = "Bio12", main = "edge")

add_data(virt_edge, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#0004d5", pch = 16, cex = 0.4)

## Uniform
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, lwd = 2, xlim = xlim_v, ylim = ylim_v,
               xlab = "Bio1", ylab = "Bio12", main = "uniform")

add_data(virt_unif, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#0004d5", pch = 16, cex = 0.4)
```

<br>

As shown in the plots, `"centroid"` puts most of the points in the middle of the niche, `"edge"` leaves the middle almost empty, and `"uniform"` covers the whole ellipsoid evenly.

<br>

## Generating data from a prediction

When environmental data are available, the niche is first predicted onto them, and the data points are then drawn from the prediction with `sample_data()`. In this case, the points can only come from conditions that exist in the region. If the prediction is a raster, each point is a cell of the raster, so it has coordinates.

Below we show a general example of how to use this function. We will draw 100 points from the truncated suitability layer of our prediction.

```{r sample}
# Generating data from the prediction
pts_basic <- sample_data(n = 100,
                         prediction = pred_rast,
                         prediction_layer = "suitability_trunc")

# Check the first points
head(pts_basic)
```

<br>

The result is a table with the coordinates of each point and its value in the layer we used. The function also told us that it detected a truncated layer and set `strict = TRUE`. We will come back to that argument below.

To see the points in environmental space (E-space), we need their environmental values. We can get them from the layers of the prediction using the coordinates.

```{r sample_env}
# Environmental values of the points
env_basic <- terra::extract(pred_rast[[vars]], pts_basic[, c("x", "y")])

head(env_basic)
```

<br>

Now let's plot the points in geographic space (G-space) and in E-space.

```{r sample_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting area parameters and axis limits for E-space
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), cex = 0.7)
marsr <- c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 4)
lims <- list(xlim = c(15, 30), ylim = c(300, 3500))

# Points in G-space
terra::plot(pred_rast[["suitability_trunc"]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Data Points in G-space")

points(pts_basic[, c("x", "y")], pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "#e10000")

# Points in E-space
par(mar = mars)

plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, background = back_data[, vars],
               pch = ".", col_bg = "#9a9797", lwd = 2,
               fixed_lims = lims,
               xlab = "Bio1 (Mean Annual Temperature)",
               ylab = "Bio12 (Annual Precipitation)",
               main = "Data Points in E-space")

add_data(env_basic, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#e10000", pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
```

<br>

The same 100 points are shown in the two spaces. In E-space they are inside the ellipsoid, with more of them near the centroid. In G-space they are spread over the sites where those conditions are found.

<br>

### Effect of the sampling argument

As in `virtual_data()`, the argument `sampling` controls where in the niche the points are more likely to be drawn: near the centroid with `"centroid"`, near the boundary with `"edge"`, or with the same chance for every cell with `"uniform"`.

```{r sampling}
# More points near the centroid
pts_cent <- sample_data(n = 100, prediction = pred_rast,
                        prediction_layer = "suitability_trunc",
                        sampling = "centroid", verbose = FALSE)

# More points near the boundary
pts_edge <- sample_data(n = 100, prediction = pred_rast,
                        prediction_layer = "suitability_trunc",
                        sampling = "edge", verbose = FALSE)

# The same chance for every cell
pts_unif <- sample_data(n = 100, prediction = pred_rast,
                        prediction_layer = "suitability_trunc",
                        sampling = "uniform", verbose = FALSE)

# Environmental values of the points
env_cent <- terra::extract(pred_rast[[vars]], pts_cent[, c("x", "y")])
env_edge <- terra::extract(pred_rast[[vars]], pts_edge[, c("x", "y")])
env_unif <- terra::extract(pred_rast[[vars]], pts_unif[, c("x", "y")])
```

<br>

Let's check the three sets of points in E-space.

```{r sampling_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.5, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting the data points
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), cex = 0.75, mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2, 0.5))

## Centroid
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, background = back_data[, vars],
               pch = ".", col_bg = "#9a9797", lwd = 2, fixed_lims = lims,
               xlab = "Bio1", ylab = "Bio12", main = "centroid")

add_data(env_cent, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#e10000", pch = 16, cex = 0.5)

## Edge
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, background = back_data[, vars],
               pch = ".", col_bg = "#9a9797", lwd = 2, fixed_lims = lims,
               xlab = "Bio1", ylab = "Bio12", main = "edge")

add_data(env_edge, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#e10000", pch = 16, cex = 0.5)

## Uniform
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, background = back_data[, vars],
               pch = ".", col_bg = "#9a9797", lwd = 2, fixed_lims = lims,
               xlab = "Bio1", ylab = "Bio12", main = "uniform")

add_data(env_unif, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#e10000", pch = 16, cex = 0.5)
```

<br>

The patterns are similar to the ones we saw with virtual data, with one difference. Here the points are drawn from the cells of the raster, and the gray points show that those cells don't fill the ellipsoid evenly. With `"uniform"`, every cell has the same chance, so there are more points in the part of the niche that has more cells.

<br>

### Effect of the method argument

The points can also be drawn from a Mahalanobis distance layer. The argument `method` tells the function which kind of layer it is receiving, `"suitability"` (the default) or `"mahalanobis"`, and it has to agree with the layer.

```{r method}
# Points drawn from the truncated Mahalanobis distance layer
pts_maha <- sample_data(n = 100, prediction = pred_rast,
                        prediction_layer = "Mahalanobis_trunc",
                        sampling = "centroid", method = "mahalanobis",
                        verbose = FALSE)

# Environmental values of the points
env_maha <- terra::extract(pred_rast[[vars]], pts_maha[, c("x", "y")])
```

<br>

Let's compare these points with the ones we drew from suitability, both with `sampling = "centroid"`.

```{r method_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting the data points
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), cex = 0.6, mar = mars)  # set up the plotting area

## Suitability
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, background = back_data[, vars],
               pch = ".", col_bg = "#9a9797", lwd = 2, fixed_lims = lims,
               xlab = "Bio1 (Mean Annual Temperature)",
               ylab = "Bio12 (Annual Precipitation)",
               main = "Method: Suitability")

add_data(env_cent, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#e10000", pch = 16, cex = 0.7)

## Mahalanobis distance
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, background = back_data[, vars],
               pch = ".", col_bg = "#9a9797", lwd = 2, fixed_lims = lims,
               xlab = "Bio1 (Mean Annual Temperature)",
               ylab = "Bio12 (Annual Precipitation)",
               main = "Method: Mahalanobis")

add_data(env_maha, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#e10000", pch = 16, cex = 0.7)
```

<br>

Both methods put more points near the centroid, but the patterns are different. With suitability, the points form a cloud around the centroid. With Mahalanobis distance, there is a tight group of points at the centroid and the rest are spread over the niche. See [The two methods give different patterns](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/concepts.html#the-two-methods-give-different-patterns) in the Concepts vignette for an explanation.

<br>

### Effect of the strict argument

In a truncated layer, the cells outside the niche have a value of 0 (suitability) or `NA` (Mahalanobis distance). The argument `strict` controls what happens with those cells. With `strict = TRUE`, they are removed before the points are drawn, so all the points are inside the niche.

If `strict` is not set, the function decides on its own. It uses `strict = TRUE` when the name of the layer contains "trunc", or when at least a quarter of the values are zero or missing. That is what happened in the examples above.

To see why this argument matters, let's draw points near the boundary of the niche without removing those cells.

```{r strict}
# Points near the boundary, keeping the cells outside the niche
pts_loose <- sample_data(n = 100, prediction = pred_rast,
                         prediction_layer = "suitability_trunc",
                         sampling = "edge", strict = FALSE,
                         verbose = FALSE)

# Environmental values of the points
env_loose <- terra::extract(pred_rast[[vars]], pts_loose[, c("x", "y")])
```

<br>

Let's compare these points with the ones we drew before with `sampling = "edge"`, where `strict` was set to `TRUE` by the function.

```{r strict_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting the data points, with wider axis limits to show the whole region
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), cex = 0.6, mar = mars)  # set up the plotting area
lims_wide <- list(xlim = c(3, 30), ylim = c(200, 7200))

## Cells outside the niche removed
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, background = back_data[, vars],
               pch = ".", col_bg = "#9a9797", lwd = 2, fixed_lims = lims_wide,
               xlab = "Bio1 (Mean Annual Temperature)",
               ylab = "Bio12 (Annual Precipitation)",
               main = "strict = TRUE")

add_data(env_edge, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#e10000", pch = 16, cex = 0.7)

## Cells outside the niche kept
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, background = back_data[, vars],
               pch = ".", col_bg = "#9a9797", lwd = 2, fixed_lims = lims_wide,
               xlab = "Bio1 (Mean Annual Temperature)",
               ylab = "Bio12 (Annual Precipitation)",
               main = "strict = FALSE")

add_data(env_loose, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#e10000", pch = 16, cex = 0.7)
```

<br>

With `strict = FALSE`, most of the points are outside the niche. With `"edge"`, a cell with low suitability gets a high chance of being drawn, and the cells outside the niche have a suitability of 0, the lowest possible. To keep the points inside the niche, use a truncated layer and `strict = TRUE`. This is most important with `"edge"` and `"uniform"`.

<br>

### Generating data from a table

`sample_data()` also works when the prediction is a table. This is useful when the environmental data are a list of sites. As an example, we will predict the reference niche onto the background table and draw points from the result.

```{r table}
# Prediction of the reference niche for the background table
pred_table <- predict(ref_ellipse, newdata = back_data,
                      suitability_truncated = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

# Generating data from the table
pts_table <- sample_data(n = 100, prediction = pred_table,
                         prediction_layer = "suitability_trunc",
                         verbose = FALSE)

# Check the first points
head(pts_table)
```

<br>

Each data point is a row of the table, with all its columns, so the environmental values come with the points and there is no need to extract them. Our table has the columns `x` and `y`, and they were kept as coordinates. A table without coordinates can also be used. In that case the points can only be shown in E-space, and the function gives a warning to let us know.

<br>

## Generating biased data

The last option is to draw the points from a prediction that was combined with sampling bias. The surface we loaded at the beginning was obtained with `apply_bias()` from the suitability of the reference niche and a bias surface. Its values are the weights used to draw the points, so the `sample_biased_data()` function only needs the surface and the number of points.

```{r biased}
# Generating data from the biased surface
pts_bias <- sample_biased_data(n = 100,
                               prediction = biased_rast,
                               prediction_layer = "suitability_centroid_biased")

# Check the first points
head(pts_bias)
```

<br>

This function has no `sampling` or `method` arguments. Those choices were made in `apply_bias()`, when the surface was created.

To see the effect of the bias, we will compare these points with points drawn from the same suitability layer without bias.

```{r unbiased}
# Generating data from suitability, without bias
pts_nobias <- sample_data(n = 100, prediction = pred_rast,
                          prediction_layer = "suitability",
                          sampling = "centroid", verbose = FALSE)

# Environmental values of the two sets of points
env_bias <- terra::extract(pred_rast[[vars]], pts_bias[, c("x", "y")])
env_nobias <- terra::extract(pred_rast[[vars]], pts_nobias[, c("x", "y")])
```

<br>

Let's plot the two sets of points in G-space and in E-space.

```{r biased_plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6, out.width = "95%"}
# Plotting area parameters
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), cex = 0.6)

# Points without bias in G-space
terra::plot(pred_rast[["suitability"]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "Without Bias in G-space")

points(pts_nobias[, c("x", "y")], pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "#e10000")

# Points with bias in G-space
terra::plot(biased_rast[["suitability_centroid_biased"]],
            axes = FALSE, box = TRUE, mar = marsr,
            main = "With Bias in G-space")

points(pts_bias[, c("x", "y")], pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = "#e10000")

# Points without bias in E-space
par(mar = mars)

plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, background = back_data[, vars],
               pch = ".", col_bg = "#9a9797", lwd = 2, fixed_lims = lims,
               xlab = "Bio1 (Mean Annual Temperature)",
               ylab = "Bio12 (Annual Precipitation)",
               main = "Without Bias in E-space")

add_data(env_nobias, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#e10000", pch = 16, cex = 0.7)

# Points with bias in E-space
plot_ellipsoid(ref_ellipse, background = back_data[, vars],
               pch = ".", col_bg = "#9a9797", lwd = 2, fixed_lims = lims,
               xlab = "Bio1 (Mean Annual Temperature)",
               ylab = "Bio12 (Annual Precipitation)",
               main = "With Bias in E-space")

add_data(env_bias, x = "bio_1", y = "bio_12",
         pts_col = "#e10000", pch = 16, cex = 0.7)
```

<br>

The clearest change is in G-space. Without bias, the points follow suitability, and many of them are in the north of the region. With bias, more of the points are in the south, where sampling effort is higher in our bias surface. In E-space the two sets look alike in this example, because the sites with more sampling effort have conditions similar to the rest of the niche. This is not always the case. When sampling effort is concentrated in sites with particular conditions, the bias also changes how the niche looks in E-space.

A few points can fall outside the ellipsoid in these plots. The layer `suitability` is not truncated, so the cells outside the niche keep a small chance of being drawn. To keep all the points inside the niche, create the biased surface from a truncated layer, as shown in [3. Working with bias](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/bias.html#keeping-the-weights-inside-the-niche).

<br>

```{r par_reset}
# Reset plotting parameters
par(original_par)
```

<br>

## Save and import

The data points are tables, so they can be saved with `write.csv()` and imported with `read.csv()`. The points drawn from a raster can be saved together with their environmental values.

```{r save_import, eval=FALSE}
# file names (in a temporary directory for demonstration purposes)
temp_virtual <- file.path(tempdir(), "virtual_data.csv")
temp_points <- file.path(tempdir(), "data_points.csv")

# Save virtual data
write.csv(virt_data, file = temp_virtual, row.names = FALSE)

# Save data points with their environmental values
write.csv(cbind(pts_basic, env_basic[, vars]), file = temp_points,
          row.names = FALSE)

# Import the data
virt_data_imported <- read.csv(temp_virtual)
pts_basic_imported <- read.csv(temp_points)
```
